children.text: The Clinton administration threw its support behind the North American Development Bank, or NADBank, a border and community development financing mechanism proposed by Latino supporters of NAFTA and championed by Congressman Esteban Torres, who said it addressed legitimate fears that free trade could harm workers and local economies. A Southwest Voter Research Institute poll found a slim majority of registered Latino/a voters supporting NAFTA, with a large share still undecided. Destructive wildfires across Southern California prompted a federal disaster declaration, with observers noting that the economic damage would affect all Californians, even though Latino/a-heavy areas were not the primary zones hit. In the Miami mayoral race, Cuban-born Commissioner Miriam Alonso was facing former mayor Steve Clark in a bitter campaign marked by personal attacks on both sides. A gang summit in Chicago aimed at building Black and Brown unity drew little Latino/a participation, with community organizer Juan Rangel calling it largely a publicity stunt while still expressing disappointment at the absence of Latino gangs. And the CDC reported measles at a record low nationally, though 224 cases in Puerto Rico were excluded from the count.

California voters were weighing Proposition 174, a school voucher initiative that would give each student $2,600 in state funds to use at private or religious schools. Supporters argued it would give parents in struggling public schools real leverage to demand improvement. Opponents, including MALDEF, LULAC, and the Latino Issues Forum, said the measure would drain more than a billion dollars from public education over three years, including funds for the 36 percent of California students who are Latino/a, and that the voucher amount was too small to provide access to quality private schools. Polls showed the measure heading toward defeat.
New York Mayoral Race and the Latino Vote

With incumbent David Dinkins and challenger Rudolph Giuliani running neck and neck, analysts said the Latino/a vote could decide New York City's mayoral contest. Dinkins campaigned on his record of Latino/a appointments and drew support from Congress members Jose Serrano and Nydia Velazquez, while Giuliani courted Latino voters through running mate Herman Badillo, a longtime Democratic political figure who had crossed party lines. Community activists used the close race to demand accountability on issues including the racial murder of a Dominican teenager and the fire bombing of a Puerto Rican family's home in Brooklyn. Voters interviewed were divided, with some prioritizing crime and others expressing loyalty to the city's first African American mayor.
Dia de los Muertos in San Francisco

The Mission District's annual Day of the Dead procession drew a large and diverse crowd celebrating the Aztec-rooted tradition of honoring the deceased through festivity rather than mourning. Participants reflected on the celebration's growing presence in the United States and its role in preserving indigenous cultural memory among Chicano/a and Latino/a communities.
Noche de Muertos: Chicano Art in Boulder

An exhibition called Noche de Muertos: Chicano Journey into Michoacan Night, on view at the University of Colorado and traveling to the Museo de las Americas in Denver, brought together Chicano/a artists responding to their 1991 journey to Patzcuaro and Tzintzuntzan in Michoacan. Works included paintings of nighttime cemeteries, collaborative altars honoring deceased grandmothers, a tribute to Ritchie Valens, and a UFW-shaped altar commemorating Cesar Chavez and Dolores Huerta. Co-curator George Rivera described the project as a way to document and transmit to future generations how their ancestors understood and honored death. The exhibit was scheduled to travel to Amsterdam and other European cities in 1995.
